items.why: The negated action contrasts clearly with what Jeroboam does again, though “not” makes the answer easy to spot.
The message originated with the man of God, but the question’s “he says” makes the attribution awkwardly ambiguous.
The passage distinguishes Jonathan’s single victory from the collective defeat by David and his men.
Resolving “him” to the officer rather than the nearer man of God is the key relation.
The sons saddle the donkey, but the old prophet is the one who mounts it.
The first covenant includes the Lord, unlike the immediately following covenant between king and people.
The burial is followed by Jotham’s succession, while Isaiah’s recording is mentioned earlier.
The explicit reason for Uzziah’s eagerness is affliction, not the priests’ simultaneous effort to remove him.
The Arameans’ nested plan clearly places entering the city after capturing the people.
The men reject entering the city and decide instead to surrender at the Aramean camp.
The two similar battles require preserving their order to identify Sibbekai as the first killer.
“The news” is vague and nearly tautological, while reporting a camp is not a natural competing answer.
The command “Seize him” targets the man of God, not the king who issues it.
Azariah is part of the group following Uzziah, making subject and object roles essential.
The today-versus-tomorrow contrast is clean but can be answered by locating a single time token.
Zechariah instructs Uzziah, whereas Amaziah is only the model whose conduct Uzziah follows.
Elisha’s reply to the doubt is the seeing-without-eating warning, not the earlier price prediction.
The refusal is explicitly grounded in the Lord’s command, though the half-possession competitor is weak.
The final action before departure is talking until daylight, with eating occurring earlier.
The sentence clearly orders mobilizing the army before marching and laying siege.
Jehoiada gives the weapons, while David is only their former owner.
The accusers are ordered to present the case; the Sanhedrin is merely the earlier venue.
The purpose of taking Uzziah is coronation, while Amaziah’s death supplies temporal background.
The 2,600 family leaders directly command the army, unlike the officials who organized its muster.
The moving pronouns must be traced from the prophet who saddles the donkey to the man of God who departs and dies.
The officer is assigned to the gate and trampled there, while the king only made the assignment.
The instructions sharply distinguish the two off-duty companies guarding the temple from the three on-duty companies.
The From/To structure identifies Claudius as writer and Felix as recipient, though the short header permits token-level lookup.
Abishai rescues David by killing Ishbi-Benob, so reversing beneficiary and victim yields the competitor.
After recognizing their wrongdoing, the men plan to report immediately rather than repeat their earlier hiding.
Paul explicitly says the young man has something to tell the commander.
The messengers’ return and report immediately precede the people’s plundering.
The final causal clause attributes love of soil to Uzziah, though the question is somewhat unnatural.
The speaker’s son is eaten first, while the other woman hides her own son the next day.
The king requests prayer, but the man of God performs it.
God helps Uzziah against three named peoples, whereas the Ammonites instead bring him tribute.
The body is taken first to the prophet’s city and only afterward placed in his tomb.
Joash is hidden with his nurse; Ahaziah is his dead father and cannot fill that role.
The text explicitly grounds the city’s calm in Athaliah’s death, not merely the people’s rejoicing.
The two centurions receive the order, while the two hundred soldiers are part of what they must prepare.
The Arameans think the hired Hittite and Egyptian kings will attack, not the Israelite king who hired them.
“This murderer” refers to the messenger’s master, the king, rather than the approaching messenger.
Within the old prophet’s claimed quotation, “him” designates the man of God who is to eat and drink.
Paul speaks late because he plans to leave, while the lamps are unrelated scene detail.
The soldiers return while the cavalry continues, though cavalry can loosely be called soldiers.
The seven sons are beaten and flee; the possessed man is the attacker.
The wording about items’ “arrival” is strained, and illnesses are cured rather than presented as literally leaving.
The Sanhedrin is to petition the commander, who is the person expected to bring Paul.
The practitioners burn the scrolls immediately after gathering them; valuation follows afterward.
The explicit sword order targets anyone following the woman, although the woman is also killed later.
Hearing the noise causes Athaliah to go; seeing the king occurs only after she arrives.
The ambushers are waiting for the commander’s consent, though Paul’s later transfer is also part of their plan.
The warning is addressed to the man of God, whose body—not the speaking prophet’s—will lack ancestral burial.
The prophecy names Josiah as the future killer, while Jeroboam is merely present at the altar.
